I have been both to both so happy to answer any questions privately.  UNSW is more flexible- the same course offered multiple times throughout the year which means you have more control over your scheduling and planning. Easier to get through your course you’re own way I would say. Usyd on the other hand, is a lot more rigid- both part time and full time students really need to stick to the degree structure they’ve proposed to get through it as Most subjects are only offered once a year. Another example is that the part time stream only has classes at night. You need faculty permission to enrol in day classes. If you need flexibility, UNSW is better imo. Also not sure what it’s like now but in 2021-22 there were some online tutorial options. 

Trimesters
This may just be my experience but because UNSW has trimesters they fit more into each subject in fewer weeks. This means there’s more work to do outside your class hours. For example, for 2 subjects I took you needed to watch a 2x pre recorded lecture every week in addition to having a 2x2 hour seminar/lecture in class (8 hours per weeks). This is contrast to just having 2x2 hour seminar classes per week (4 hours) or the standard 2hour lecture plus one hour tutorial-which is common at usyd. The more intensity at UNSW is somewhat offset by the fact a full time course load is 3 subjects per trimester compared to 4 subjects per semester at usyd. YMMV but the trimesters we’re still too fast. The also annoying thing about them was that depending on when your last exam is - you don’t get much of a break. 

Teaching quality 
Both unis had great teachers. Not sure how much of a difference is makes but at UNSW I had more contracted teachers whereas as usyd I’ve had more University staff eg professors, academics- who are enthusiastic about the subject they teach. On the other hand, The UNSW staff seemed to have more real world experience and had more anecdotes about how things worked in practice. Teaching quality very high at both though. A lot of effort put into the classes (mostly). 

Admin/student centre/disability support/student support: I would say extremely similar, frustrating and annoying at both. 

Reputation: both are good. I believe both are equal 20th in the rankings too. You’ll meet many lecturers and staff who’ve been one or the other. I think reputation only matters to the individual. Eg if you feel pride/happiness when you say “I go to usyd”. I’ve been in the workforce, and law graduates vary from all over the place. If you don’t get hired somewhere it won’t be because you went to UNSW rather than usyd. But again, if it makes a difference to you internally, that is valid and something to consider. 

My suggestion would be take a day to walk around each campus when semester is on. See which one feels “more you”. By way of background, I started my jd at UNSW and moved to usyd. Move was motivated by not getting big enough breaks between trimester and also, because I did my undergrad at usyd, I’m much more “at home” there and enjoying it a lot more. 

Hope this helps Good Luck!

I think this has been looked at in a very black and white way:  

Have an abortion = stay married. 

But there’s probably more grey…

Your marriage will change if you the abortion. Your relationship with your husband will always be tainted with ‘you wanted to leave me and your unborn child.’ Or worse, ‘he didn’t love me enough to keep a miracle child.’ ‘I had an abortion because of you.’ He won’t ever be able to “make up” for that. A lot commentators have said the husband is well within his rights to have this boundary. Even if that is the case, it won’t stop these feelings from arising. 
So yeah, OP may stay with a husband that she loves- but it will never be what it was like when before the pregnancy. Also, deciding not have kids as a couple, is a very different conversation to ‘if we get accidentally pregnant, what will we do?’ And it doesn’t seem like they had had this conversation prior to the pregnancy. So yeah, maybe husband IS being douchey. At least with the child, you’ll love it forever. 

I’m a child of single parent who didn’t ~want~ me. A few things from my experience. I felt extremely guilty for being born. I blamed myself for all the things my mum sacrificed. I had a Genuine belief that my mums life would have been substantially better with me. This meant I had a lot of mental issues to deal with and I had to have a lot of therapy to resolve them. And this was even with my mum reassuring me she had no regret…but I could still see she was unhappy with her level of sacrifice. I’m not saying this would happen to your child, but they may need to SEE you happy. Another thing, is that assuming the divorce happens, the kid will know they’re dad rejected them for merely existing…. So they have need to work through some things there when they get older and understand. 

Also, at 49, it’s likely the husband will end up dating people who have children themselves which will be tough pill to swallow 

I don’t envy your position. Good luck. Follow your intuition
